title: Short Stuff: Victorian Flower Language
summary: Short Stuff episode on Victorian floriography, the coded language of flowers. Josh and Chuck open with playful banter in which they send each other flower messages (a nosegay, upside-down delivery, ribbon placement). They trace the practice to the Ottoman Harem's selam flower game, which Lady Mary Wortley Montagu described in letters that carried it to Britain. They cover nosegays and tussie-mussies, herbs' meanings, and flower color meanings (red rose, white rose, yellow rose, crimson rose, thornless rose, hydrangea, petunia). They explain that context matters, that many competing floriography books existed (about 98 guides in the US from 1827 to 1923), and that meaning depended on how a bouquet was presented, tied, and accepted (right vs. left hand, upside down). They also cover negative meanings (marigold, lavender, orange lily, snapdragon, tansy, wisteria) and carnation replies. Jane Austen's use of flower symbolism is mentioned, with a Pride and Prejudice red rose passage. The episode closes with the nosegay-placement joke and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and flower-message jokes
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode by jokingly referencing a nosegay of wilted white roses sent upside down with the ribbon to the left, and riff on whether it meant something about where it was worn.

segments.title: What floriography is and why it was popular
segments.summary: Josh explains floriography as the practice of sending unspoken messages with flowers, popular in the Victorian and Regency periods. Chuck explains it was a workaround for topics that could not be spoken openly in polite society, mainly among upper-class women. Josh thanks the research sources.

segments.title: Origins in the Ottoman Empire and Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
segments.summary: Chuck describes the selam game in the Harem of Constantinople, where flowers with rhymes and meanings were exchanged. Josh says Lady Mary Wortley, wife of the British ambassador to Turkey, wrote letters describing the selam custom, which spread the practice to Britain.

segments.title: Puns aside
segments.summary: A short exchange in which Chuck and Josh talk about puns from an earlier episode, the Operation Paul Bunyan episode, before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Jane Austen and flower symbolism in literature
segments.summary: Chuck asks whether Jane Austen fans would notice flower messages in her books. Josh says Austen and the Brontë sisters used floriography to develop characters, and that modern readers would miss it. Josh reads a Pride and Prejudice passage in which Elizabeth Bennet gives Mr. Darcy a red rose, with the word red repeated in the text.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Nosegays, tussie-mussies, and herb meanings
segments.summary: Josh explains nosegays and tussie-mussies as small tightly bound bouquets worn at the chest, made of flowers and herbs. He lists herb meanings: rosemary for remembrance, mint for clarity, moss for charity or maternal love, and violet for modesty. Chuck notes the combined message would be confusing.

segments.title: Flower and rose color meanings
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh go through flower color meanings: yellow carnation or rose for rejection, yellow lily for being over the moon, red rose for love, white rose for purity, yellow rose for loss of love, and crimson rose for mourning. Josh adds that a withered white rose meant no impression, and a dried one meant refusal to give in to advances.

segments.title: Context and competing floriography books
segments.summary: Chuck notes thornless roses mean love at first sight and a hydrangea can mean thanks or coldness depending on context. Josh says petunias can mean soothing or resentment. He explains that multiple meanings came from many competing floriography books, and that about 98 guides circulated in the US from 1827 to 1923.

segments.title: Upside-down bouquets, ribbon placement, and negative meanings
segments.summary: Chuck explains that an upside-down bouquet signals opposite meaning and that ribbon tied left refers to the giver while tied right refers to the recipient. Josh lists negative meanings: marigold for jealousy, lavender for distrust, orange lily for hate, snapdragon for feeling deceived, and tansy for declaring war.

segments.title: Tansy and the pansy mix-up
segments.summary: Chuck says he thought tansy was a misprint for pansy. Josh confirms tansy is a real flower, a cluster of small yellow blooms.

segments.title: Accepting bouquets with left or right hand and carnation replies
segments.summary: Chuck explains that accepting flowers with the right hand meant yes and the left hand meant no, and holding a bouquet upside down meant rejection. A wisteria held upside down in the left hand declined a dance request. Josh explains that a receiver could reply with carnations: solid for yes, yellow for no, striped for a gentle no.

segments.title: Nosegay placement joke
segments.summary: Josh says wearing the nosegay at the center of the bodice meant just friends, while over the heart meant I love you. Chuck jokingly says he loves Josh as a friend.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the Short Stuff episode. A brief iHeartRadio production credit and listening note follow.
